title: Rings that tell time
teaches: How the cambium under the bark makes a ring of wood each year, and how matching patterns of wide and thin rings dates old timber

blocks.text: Andrew Ellicott Douglass came to Flagstaff, Arizona, in 1894 to help build an observatory, and stayed interested in the sun. He wondered whether the eleven-year sunspot cycle changed the weather on Earth, and there were no long weather records in Arizona to test it. Trees, he thought, might be the records. In the dry Southwest a pine grows more in a wet year than a dry one, and each year's growth is a ring in its trunk. In 1901 he began measuring the rings on ponderosa pine logs and stumps from the forests around Flagstaff.

He never found a convincing sunspot cycle. He found something more useful. The pattern of wide and thin rings was the same from tree to tree. A run of thin rings in one stump turned up, ring for ring, in a stump on the other side of town, and in stumps from forests a long day's ride away. A year that was dry around Flagstaff was dry across the region, and every tree recorded it. That meant a piece of wood could be dated by its pattern, the way a passage can be found in a book by matching a distinctive phrase.

Lesson 12 showed that a tree grows taller only at its shoot tips: a nail in a trunk stays at the height it was driven. In the 1750s the French naturalist Henri-Louis Duhamel du Monceau pushed this further. He drove nails and threaded silver wires into trunks and under the bark, and found years later that the wires in the wood had stayed in place, buried under new wood laid down outside them. A trunk thickens by adding new layers on the outside of the old ones, just under the bark.

blocks.caption: A slice across a trunk, from the bark in to the pith, the soft core left from the first year's shoot.

blocks.text: The layer that does it is the **cambium**, a sheet of dividing cells only a few cells thick, wrapped all the way round the trunk, branches and roots, just under the bark. It is a meristem like the ones at the tips (lesson 12), but it widens the stem instead of lengthening it. Cells it makes on its inner side become xylem, the wood of lesson 6. Cells it makes on its outer side become phloem, the sugar pipes of lesson 9. So the wood piles up on the inner side of the cambium, each year's layer outside the last, while the cambium itself moves outward and the old phloem is pushed out ahead of it and crushed into the bark, which is why bark stays thin and wood gets thick.

Only the outer few centimetres of wood, the **sapwood**, carry water. Further in, the cells are plugged with resins and dark chemicals that resist rot, and become **heartwood**, which no longer carries water and mainly holds the tree up. Lesson 9's girdling, cutting a strip of bark all the way round, kills a tree because it cuts the phloem, which runs just outside the cambium; a hollow tree with its heart rotted out can live for centuries, since all its living tissue is in the outer layers.

In spring, when the cambium wakes and the tree needs to move a lot of water to its new growth, it makes large, thin-walled water pipes: the pale, soft **early wood**. As summer goes on and water runs short, it makes smaller cells with thick walls: the dark, dense **late wood**. Then it stops for the winter. Next spring the large pale cells start again right against the last year's dense ones, and the sharp line between them is the edge of a ring.

blocks.caption: A young pine in a dry climate, adding a ring of wood each year from the rain the year brings. A model.
blocks.task: Grow at least eight years, with at least one dry year and one wet one

blocks.text: How wide the ring is depends on whatever is in shortest supply that year. In the dry Southwest that is water, so a wet year leaves a wide ring and a drought year leaves a ring so thin it can be hard to see. Near the tree line in the mountains, or in the far north, the short cool summer limits growth instead, and wide rings mean warm summers. Many trees in the wet tropics, with no winter and no dry season, make no clear rings at all.[^false]

Counting the rings on a stump tells you the tree's age when it was cut. Douglass wanted more: the calendar year each ring grew, for any piece of wood, including wood with no bark and no known felling date. He started with living trees, whose outermost ring is the one growing this year, so the rest can be counted back from it. Overlapping their patterns with older stumps and logs, he built a **master series**: the relative width of each year's ring, going back centuries. Any new piece of wood from the region can be dated by sliding its pattern along the master until it fits, which is called **cross-dating**.

blocks.caption: An old beam's ring widths slid along a master series. Made-up widths, with dry years as very thin rings.
blocks.task: Find the year the beam's outermost ring grew

blocks.text: It works because the thin rings are rare and irregular, so a run of them, with their spacing, is as distinctive as a fingerprint. Douglass checked his dating by finding the same thin years in tree after tree. A single tree can miss a ring in a terrible year or grow a doubled one in a strange season, and cross-dating catches these too, because the anomaly shows up in one sample when it is set against all the others.

parts.title: The beam that closed the gap

blocks.text: The pueblos of the Southwest, the great stone and adobe towns at Mesa Verde, Chaco Canyon and elsewhere, had been abandoned centuries before Europeans came, and no one knew when they were built. Their roofs were held up by pine and fir beams, many still in place. From the 1920s, Douglass's expeditions drilled into those beams with hollow bits, taking out pencil-thin cores of wood with the rings across them. The beams cross-dated with one another cleanly, and he built a second master series from them, nearly 600 years long, that put the ruins in order. But it floated: it matched nothing in his master series from living trees. His dated series, counted back from living trees and old Hopi beams, went back to about 1260, and the floating series ended at some unknown date. Nothing joined them.

On 22 June 1929, at a ruin being dug at Show Low, Arizona, his team pulled out a charred log catalogued as HH-39. Its inner, older rings matched the outer part of the floating series, and its outer, younger rings matched the earliest years of the dated one. Actually, there was no gap at all: the two series had already overlapped by a couple of decades, though with too few rings in common to be sure until HH-39 tied them together. That evening, Douglass could put calendar years on the ruins he had measured. Pueblo Bonito at Chaco had been built in stages from the mid-800s to the early 1100s. The cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde were built mostly in the 1200s and abandoned by about 1285, during a run of very thin rings from 1276 to 1299 that Douglass called the Great Drought. Later work has confirmed the drought, though it was probably one of several reasons people left.

Tree-ring series now run back far longer. Bristlecone pines in the White Mountains of California, which can live nearly 5,000 years, have been joined with dead wood on the slopes around them into a series going back nearly 9,000 years, and oaks and pines preserved in European river gravels and bogs go back more than 12,000.[^prometheus] Those series were used to check and calibrate radiocarbon dating,[^radiocarbon] since once a tree-ring series is cross-dated, every ring's calendar year is known.[^cascadia]

Lesson 12's nail stays where it was driven, and Duhamel's wires end up buried in wood; both point to the same way of growing. A tree adds a new layer outside the old one every year and never moves the old ones. Since the tree also grows taller each year at its tip, each year's layer reaches higher than the one inside it. The trunk is a stack of long thin cones of wood, one for each year, nested inside each other, with the newest on the outside.

Find a fresh stump, or a round of firewood with a clean cut. Count the rings from the bark in, marking every tenth with a pencil. If you know when the tree was cut, the ring next to the bark is that year, and you can count back to see what years the narrow rings were. A run of wide rings after narrow ones near the centre often means the tree was released, when a bigger neighbour fell and gave it light. A ring that is wide on one side and narrow on the other usually means the tree grew leaning, and laid down extra wood, called reaction wood, to hold itself up.

blocks.caption: Six questions on wood and rings
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Where does a tree's new wood form each year?
choices: Just inside the bark, from the cambium
At the centre of the trunk
items.why: The cambium, a thin layer of dividing cells under the bark, adds xylem (wood) on its inside and phloem on its outside.

items.ask: What makes the visible edge of each ring?
choices: Dense late-summer wood next to the next spring's large pale cells
A layer of bark buried each winter
items.why: Late in the season the cambium makes small thick-walled cells; next spring it starts again with large thin-walled ones, and the contrast is sharp.

items.ask: In the dry Southwest, what does a very thin ring usually mean?
items.why: Where water limits growth, a dry year means little new wood.

items.ask: How is an old beam with no bark and no known felling date given calendar years?
choices: By matching its pattern of wide and thin rings against a dated master series
By counting its rings from the centre
items.why: Counting gives only its length of life. Cross-dating against a master series built back from living trees fixes each ring to a year.

items.ask: Why was beam HH-39 so important to Douglass in 1929?
choices: Its rings overlapped both the undated ruin series and the dated series, joining them
It was the oldest beam ever found
It proved sunspots change tree growth
items.why: It bridged the undated series from the ruins and the master series from living trees, so every ruin beam in the series could be dated.

items.ask: Why can a tree survive with its centre rotted away?
choices: Its living tissue, the cambium, phloem and sapwood, is in the outer layers
Heartwood carries most of its water
items.why: Heartwood is dead and only holds the tree up. Water, sugar and growth are all in the outermost few centimetres.

summary: **A trunk thickens by adding layers outside the old ones.** Duhamel's nails and wires (1750s) stayed put and were buried by new wood.
**The cambium makes wood inside and phloem outside.** It is a thin sheet of dividing cells all round the trunk under the bark.
**Each ring is a year's wood.** Large pale spring cells, then dense late-summer cells, then a winter stop.
**Ring width records the year.** In dry places a wet year makes a wide ring; near the tree line, a warm summer does.
**Cross-dating matches patterns, not counts.** The pattern of thin rings is shared by every tree in a region.
**HH-39 joined Douglass's two series (1929).** The Southwest's ruins got calendar dates, and the Great Drought of 1276 to 1299 showed up.
**Sapwood carries water; heartwood mainly holds the tree up.** All the living tissue is in the outer layers.

false.title: Missing and false rings
false.text: In a very bad year a tree may lay down no wood at all on part of its trunk, so a ring is missing there. A summer drought broken by late rain can make the cambium switch to dense wood and back again, leaving a false ring inside the true one. Cross-dating against many trees finds both.

cascadia.title: The ghost forest
cascadia.text: Along the Washington coast stand the dead trunks of western redcedars killed when the land dropped and the sea flooded their roots in a great earthquake. Their outermost rings show they grew through the summer of 1699 and never grew again, so the earthquake struck between autumn 1699 and spring 1700. Records of a tsunami that reached Japan narrowed it to the evening of 26 January 1700 (Geology's Cascadia lesson).

prometheus.title: Prometheus
prometheus.text: In 1964 a geographer studying ice-age moraines on Wheeler Peak in Nevada, with permission from the US Forest Service, cut down a gnarled bristlecone pine known as Prometheus after his coring drills stuck or proved too short. Counting the slab that night, he found at least 4,862 rings: he had felled the oldest known non-clonal tree then living.

radiocarbon.title: Radiocarbon dating
radiocarbon.text: Radiocarbon dating measures how much radioactive carbon-14 remains in dead organic matter such as wood, charcoal or bone. Because the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has varied slightly from century to century, raw radiocarbon ages drift from true calendar years; testing wood from dated tree rings allowed physicists to build a calibration curve to correct them.
